passage: In the office creche, Simran, five, had the animal puzzles. Kiran came over. Yesterday Kiran had given her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple. Simran pushed the box across at once. "You can do the lion. You gave me red." Then Babloo came, the boy who kept the blocks under his mat every day. "Give me the elephant." Simran put both hands on the box. "No. You never give me blocks." Babloo stamped his foot. The creche didi sat down. "Babloo, what could you share?" Babloo looked at his mat, then pushed two blocks over.

qa.q: What did Kiran give Simran yesterday?
qa.a: Kiran gave her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple.

qa.q: Why did Simran put both hands on the box when Babloo asked?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at the unfairness of giving to Babloo, who keeps the blocks under his mat every day and never shares.

qa.q: How did the creche didi help, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked Babloo what he could share, which let him see that giving makes others want to give back.

qa.q: How might Babloo feel when Simran refuses him?
qa.a: Babloo may feel angry and left out at first, which is why he stamps his foot, before realising he could share too.

grounding: A five-year-old shares with a friend who shared before and refuses a child who never shares, showing early 'you did for me, I do for you' fairness.

passage: I'm Charu, Mridul's big sister. On Sunday the building kids played in our hall. Mridul, five, had his new remote car. Guddu asked first. Last week Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages. Mridul gave him the remote at once. "You gave me bubbles, so you drive." Then Sonu stuck his hand out. Sonu never lets anyone touch his football. Mridul hid the remote. "No. You don't share, so I don't share." Sonu went red and sat by the door. Mridul kept looking at him. After Guddu's turn he walked over. "Bring your football next time."

qa.q: What had Guddu let Mridul do last week?
qa.a: Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been thinking when he kept looking at Sonu?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sorry for Sonu sitting alone, while still believing that sharing should go both ways.

qa.q: Which choice at the end helped, and why?
qa.a: Saying 'Bring your football next time' gave Sonu a way to join the give-and-take instead of being left out for good.

qa.q: How might Sonu feel sitting by the door?
qa.a: Sonu likely feels embarrassed and left out, seeing Guddu enjoy the car while he is refused.

grounding: A five-year-old shares his toy with a friend who shared before and refuses one who never shares, as told by his older sister.

passage: Minakshi, nine, and Hafsa washed Mr Kapoor's car every Sunday in their Lucknow colony. This Sunday, Mr Kapoor gave Minakshi sixty rupees and Hafsa forty. "For my neighbour's girl, a little extra," he winked. Minakshi's face went hot. "That's not fair! Hafsa did the wheels and the mats. I only did the windows. She should get more!" Mr Kapoor laughed. "It's only twenty rupees, beta." "It's the rule," Minakshi said, and pushed twenty rupees into Hafsa's hand. That night she opened her notebook. Every Sunday had a line: who did wheels, who did windows, who brought the bucket. Hafsa, reading over her shoulder, giggled. "You even wrote the bucket?" "Somebody has to keep it fair," Minakshi said, underlining it twice.

qa.q: How much money did Mr Kapoor first give Minakshi?
qa.a: He gave Minakshi sixty rupees.

qa.q: Why was Minakshi upset even though she got more money?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Hafsa had done the wheels and the mats, which was more work than her windows.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's notebook do well, and where could it go too far?
qa.a: It helps her keep things fair, but counting even the bucket every week could turn a fun friendship into a strict account.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Minakshi's notebook?
qa.a: Hafsa finds it funny that her friend writes down even who brought the bucket, though she also benefits from Minakshi's sense of fairness.

grounding: A nine-year-old refuses an unequal payment in her favour and keeps a strict notebook of who did what, showing an emerging, rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
"Nani, you gave me thirty and Nikhil twenty." Ankita, ten, held up the coins.
"You fetched the vegetables, beti."
"But Nikhil fetched the milk twice and the newspaper. That's three trips. I only did one."
Nikhil, eight, looked up hopefully. "She's right, Nani."
"Arrey, it's just pocket money."
"It's not fair if it's not counted." Ankita took out a sheet of paper. "I'm making a chart. Trips, sweeping, watering plants. Each gets five rupees."
"And who checks the chart?" Nani asked, amused.
"Me."
"And if I give you extra because you're my first grandchild?"
"Then I'll give it to Nikhil." Ankita slid ten rupees across the table.
Nani shook her head, smiling. "This girl will run a bank one day."
Nikhil pocketed the coins before anyone could change their mind.

qa.q: What did Ankita fetch for Nani?
qa.a: She fetched the vegetables.

qa.q: What does Ankita's chart suggest about how she feels about fairness?
qa.a: It suggests she is determined that fairness means counting exactly, even when counting leaves her with less.

qa.q: How could Nani help Ankita keep fairness without making it rigid?
qa.a: She could praise Ankita's honesty and also explain that small gifts of love don't always need to be counted like payments.

qa.q: How does Nikhil see Ankita's rule?
qa.a: Nikhil is happy and a bit surprised, since Ankita's strict counting gives Nikhil more money.

grounding: A ten-year-old objects to an unequal split in her favour and makes a strict chart of chores, showing a strong but rigid sense of fairness.

passage: When Zanele's laptop broke in March, Alejandro lent her his old one for the whole term. He even set it up for her and showed her how to recover a lost essay. Zanele, fifteen, was grateful. At first. Then every time she opened the lid in her room in Johannesburg, she felt a small weight. What had she given back? A packet of biscuits. That didn't count. When Alejandro asked her to help him with his history project, she said yes at once, though she had two tests that week. At lunch he joked, "Zanele owes me a kidney." Everyone laughed, and so did she. But on the walk home the joke stayed with her, and she felt a flash of resentment she didn't like, as if their friendship had turned into a bill she could never pay.

qa.q: What did Alejandro lend Zanele?
qa.a: He lent her his old laptop for the whole term.

qa.q: What did Zanele feel when she heard Alejandro's joke?
qa.a: She felt a flash of resentment and guilt, as if their friendship had become a bill she could never pay.

qa.q: What could Zanele try instead of silently counting her debt?
qa.a: She could thank Alejandro openly, help him with his history project in a way that suits her time, and tell him the joke made her uneasy.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see the laptop he lent?
qa.a: He may see it as a simple kindness and not realise his joke made Zanele feel she owed him.

grounding: A teenager who received a big favour feels a pull to return it, and guilt and resentment when she cannot, as the friendship starts to feel like a ledger.

passage: In the school's coding lab, Arohi had spent three lunch breaks helping Parul fix her robot's sensor for the science exhibition. Parul, fourteen, won second prize. She thanked Arohi twice and bought her a samosa. Still, it didn't feel enough. On Monday Arohi said, "Can you do my library duty on Thursday? I've got dance practice." Parul said yes, though Thursday was her only free period. The next week Arohi asked again. Parul said yes again. By the third time, Parul felt a knot in her stomach when she saw Arohi coming. She liked Arohi. She owed her. But each favour seemed to open a new line in some book only she could see. Sitting alone at the library desk, stamping books, she wondered when she would be allowed to say no.

qa.q: What did Arohi help Parul fix?
qa.a: Arohi helped Parul fix the robot's sensor for the science exhibition.

qa.q: Why did Parul feel a knot in her stomach when she saw Arohi coming?
qa.a: She felt she still owed Arohi for the robot help, so she felt guilty saying no and a bit resentful at being asked again.

qa.q: What could Parul say to Arohi to protect the friendship?
qa.a: She could thank Arohi warmly again and say she can't take library duty every week, so helping doesn't become a debt she keeps paying.

qa.q: How might Arohi see the favours asked of Parul?
qa.a: Arohi may see them as small, friendly swaps and not realise Parul feels trapped by owing Arohi.

grounding: A teenager who received help feels obliged to keep repaying it, and guilt and resentment grow as the friendship starts to feel like a ledger.

passage: I'm Jeevan. In our second year we were five people sharing a co-living flat in Bengaluru, and I noticed the pattern with Irawati before anyone said it aloud. She took rides in Kiran's scooter, ate the parathas Meera's mother sent, used my printer for every assignment. When it was her turn to buy cooking gas, she "forgot". Twice. Nobody confronted her. Instead, things just stopped. Meera started hiding the paratha box in her room. Kiran said he was "going the other way" every time Irawati needed a ride. And one night, when Irawati asked to print again, Meera said, loudly, "Printer's only for people who buy paper." Everyone went quiet. I didn't say anything either. Looking back, we all punished her with silence and hints for months before anyone just talked to her.

qa.q: What did Irawati "forget" to do twice?
qa.a: She forgot to buy cooking gas when it was her turn.

qa.q: What does Jeevan feel now, looking back on how the flat treated Irawati?
qa.a: Jeevan seems uneasy, noticing that everyone, including Jeevan, punished her with silence and hints instead of speaking to her directly.

qa.q: What could the flatmates have done before hiding things and making pointed comments?
qa.a: They could have sat down with Irawati early and asked her to share costs and chores fairly, giving her a clear chance to change.

qa.q: How might Irawati have experienced the flat after people started withdrawing?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out and confused, noticing rides and food disappear without anyone telling her why.

grounding: A flatmate notices one person keeps taking without giving and sees the group quietly withdraw and make pointed comments before anyone confronts her.

passage:
Warden's note, Girls' Hostel, 10 November. Written by Mrs Iyer.

Shalini, twenty, from Room 12, came to talk to me this evening, not to complain, she said, but because she was uneasy. In their room of four, Pooja has been borrowing everything: iron, bucket, notes, even money for the canteen, and never returning or offering anything. Shalini said the others have quietly stopped: they lock their cupboards, they leave for mess without her, and yesterday someone stuck a note on the iron saying "Ask the owner." Shalini said, "Nobody has actually told her. We just freeze her out. It's making the room cold for all of us."

What I did next: I suggested Shalini and her roommates sit together with Pooja and agree on a simple sharing list. I offered to be there if they want.

qa.q: What note did someone stick on the iron?
qa.a: Someone stuck a note on the iron saying 'Ask the owner.'

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel uneasy enough to talk to the warden?
qa.a: She was uneasy because the room was freezing Pooja out without ever telling her, and it was making the room cold for everyone.

qa.q: Why is sitting down together with Pooja a better step than the freeze-out?
qa.a: It gives Pooja a clear, fair chance to change, instead of punishing her with locked cupboards and notes she may not understand.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel about the locked cupboards and the note on the iron?
qa.a: Pooja may feel hurt and confused, or defensive, since the others have withdrawn without ever talking to her directly.

grounding: A hostel roommate notices one person keeps taking without giving and sees the group withdraw and hint before anyone confronts her.

passage: I'm Yusuf, and I'm the friend with the camera. Over the years I've lent it to half my college batch for weddings and projects, and I've covered shoots for friends who couldn't afford a photographer. I never kept a list. It felt good. But with my cousin Shalini, something changed. She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year, all paid work for her, and it came back twice with a cracked lens cap and once with the battery dead and no charger. She never offered to share the cost. When she called last month, "Yusuf bhai, one more shoot?", for a ninth time, my chest went tight; I hate disappointing family. I took a breath and said, calmly, "Shalini, I'm not lending it for paid shoots any more. You've used it a lot and never looked after it. I'm glad to help you learn to use one, though." She was annoyed for a week. I still lend it to others.

qa.q: How many shoots did Shalini borrow the camera for in a year?
qa.a: She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Shalini called the ninth time?
qa.a: His chest went tight because he hates disappointing family, yet he knew the pattern had to stop.

qa.q: Which part of Yusuf's reply made it a fair limit rather than a punishment?
qa.a: He named the exact problem calmly and offered other help, so it was a clear limit on paid shoots, not cutting her off.

qa.q: How might Shalini see the refusal once her annoyance fades?
qa.a: She may realise she took the camera for granted and that her cousin still cares, since he offered to help her learn.

grounding: A young man lends generously without keeping score, but calmly stops lending to a cousin who habitually takes, while still helping others.

passage:
Vice-principal's note, 3 March. Written by Mrs Rao.

Sudha, twenty-five, is one of our most generous teachers. She covers classes for anyone who is ill, lends her lesson plans to new staff, and never asks for anything back. This term, though, she has covered Shreya's Class 7 periods eleven times, always at short notice, and Shreya has never once covered for her. Today I overheard Sudha in the staffroom. Shreya asked her to take Friday's periods again. Sudha said, quietly and kindly, "Shreya, I've been happy to help. But it's become every week, and it only goes one way. I can't take Friday." Shreya looked startled. Sudha went back to her marking, hands steady.

What I did next: I checked the cover register and set up a fair rota so cover is shared evenly across the staff.

qa.q: How many times had Sudha covered Shreya's periods this term?
qa.a: She had covered them eleven times.

qa.q: What does Sudha's steady hands after refusing suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and sure about the limit, even though saying no to a colleague was not easy.

qa.q: What did Sudha get right in how she refused?
qa.a: She acknowledged she had been glad to help, named the one-way pattern plainly and kindly, and said no to Friday without blaming Shreya.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel about the new cover rota?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed at first but will know exactly what is expected, and the rest of the staff may feel the system is fairer.

grounding: A generous young teacher who helps freely calmly stops covering for a colleague who only takes, and a fair rota follows.

passage: I'm Parul. I was on the bench by our building's sandpit when this happened to my little cousin Kiran. He is four. Three bigger children were making a castle. Kiran ran over with his spade. "Can I help?" A girl in a pink cap said, "No. You can't play with us. You'll break it." Kiran stood very still, holding his spade. Then he walked back slowly and climbed onto the bench. "My tummy is hurting," he said, face in my arm. I held him. "That felt bad, didn't it?" He nodded. Later we dug our own tunnel.

qa.q: What was Kiran holding when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: He was holding his spade.

qa.q: What does Kiran saying his tummy hurts suggest?
qa.a: It suggests being left out made him feel a real, body-felt hurt, even though he could not name it as sad.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped Kiran?
qa.a: Parul held him, named the feeling for him and then played with him, so he felt comforted and not alone.

qa.q: Why might the girl in the pink cap have said no to Kiran?
qa.a: She may have been worried that a small child would break the castle, without noticing how much her words would hurt him.

grounding: A four-year-old told he can't play freezes and says his tummy hurts, showing exclusion felt as physical pain, as seen by his cousin.

passage:
Monday. At playschool, Minakshi, five, asked to play house. Vishal shook his head. "You can't play with us. We already have a mummy." Minakshi froze. At snack time she said her tummy hurt and left her banana.

Wednesday. Minakshi stood near the house corner, holding her stomach. The teacher sat with her. "Being left out hurts, doesn't it?" Minakshi nodded, eyes wet.

Friday. The teacher said, "Every house needs a neighbour who brings sweets." Vishal thought, then said, "You can be the neighbour." Minakshi carried plastic laddoos over. She ate her whole banana.

qa.q: What did Vishal say when Minakshi asked to play house on Monday?
qa.a: He said, 'You can't play with us. We already have a mummy.'

qa.q: What does Minakshi holding her stomach on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the hurt of being left out felt like a real pain in her body.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped by Friday?
qa.a: The teacher named Minakshi's hurt and then suggested a new role, the neighbour, so Vishal could include her without giving up his game.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when he lets Minakshi join as the neighbour?
qa.a: Vishal might feel pleased to keep his game while adding a friend, finding that including her made the play better.

grounding: A five-year-old told she can't play freezes and says her tummy hurts, showing that exclusion feels like physical pain, until a teacher helps her join.

passage: In the village school near Dharwad, Vidya, ten, walked in on Monday and said, "Hi," to her three friends. They looked at their slates. At lunch under the tamarind tree they sat in a tight circle, backs to her. Nobody said anything mean. Nobody said anything at all. By Wednesday Vidya was checking her memory for what she had done. The ribbon she forgot to return? Winning at kho-kho? Her stomach felt heavy all day. She almost wished they would shout. That evening her brother Jeevan noticed her rice going cold. "What's wrong?" Vidya burst into tears. Amma came and sat with her, listened to all of it and said, "You haven't done anything to deserve this." Then she walked with Vidya to the teacher's house that same evening to tell her.

qa.q: Where did Vidya's friends sit at lunch?
qa.a: They sat in a tight circle under the tamarind tree, with their backs to her.

qa.q: Why did Vidya almost wish her friends would shout?
qa.a: Being ignored left her confused and anxious about what she had done, and a shout would at least have told her something.

qa.q: What choice by Amma helped most, and why?
qa.a: Amma listened, told Vidya she had not deserved it and took her to the teacher that same evening, so she was not left alone with the silence.

qa.q: How did Jeevan notice something was wrong?
qa.a: He saw his sister's rice going cold, which told him she was upset even before she spoke.

grounding: A ten-year-old whose friends stop speaking to her feels invisible, anxious and confused, and her mother acts the same day.

passage: On Tuesday Abebe, eleven, said, "Hey," to Mei and the others at his table in their Melbourne classroom. Mei turned to talk to Liam as if Abebe were not there. At recess the group walked away. In science, when Abebe asked Mei to pass the ruler, she passed it to Liam instead, who dropped it by Abebe without looking. No one had teased him. Somehow that made it worse. All through maths he wondered what he had done. By lunch he felt like a ghost. He went to the library and sat under a table. Ms Walsh, the librarian, found him, sat on the floor beside him and listened. "This is not your fault," she said, and before the final bell she had spoken to his teacher and phoned his dad.

qa.q: Where did Abebe go at lunch?
qa.a: He went to the library and sat under a table.

qa.q: What does Abebe hiding under a table show about how being ignored felt?
qa.a: He says no one teased him and somehow that made it worse, and by lunch he felt like a ghost, hiding under a table.

qa.q: What did Ms Walsh do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with him, listened, told him it was not his fault and told his teacher and his dad before the day ended.

qa.q: How might Abebe's dad feel after the phone call?
qa.a: His dad would likely be worried and sad for his son but glad the school noticed quickly and acted.

grounding: A boy whose friends suddenly stop speaking to him feels invisible and confused, and a librarian responds the same day.

passage: I'm Pranav, and I go to the same dance class as Lakshmi. She's eleven and the best at spins. Last month a new girl, Sana, joined and got the front spot in the show. The next week Lakshmi whispered to all the girls in the changing room, and after that nobody stood near Sana, nobody passed her the water bottle, nobody laughed at her jokes. Lakshmi walked in front of the group, chin up, and everyone copied her. I heard her say, "She thinks she's a star. She deserves it." But I also noticed she kept glancing back to check the others were still with her, and when one girl smiled at Sana, Lakshmi's face went tight. I don't know what she was scared of. Last year Lakshmi had been the new girl nobody talked to.

qa.q: What did Sana get in the show?
qa.a: She got the front spot in the show.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi's glances back at the group suggest?
qa.a: They suggest that under her confidence she was afraid of losing her place, needing to check everyone was still following her.

qa.q: What could a teacher or friend do to stop the freeze-out?
qa.a: Someone could talk to Lakshmi privately about how she felt last year as the new girl, and pair Sana with different dancers in practice.

qa.q: What is dance class like for Sana now?
qa.a: Sana is surrounded by girls who won't stand near her or laugh at her jokes, which likely makes her feel lonely and unwanted despite her front spot.

grounding: A girl leads a group in shunning a new dancer, feels powerful and says the girl deserves it, while seeming afraid of losing her own place.

passage:
Monday. Mohit, ten, stood in the school corridor with his gang. "From today, nobody talks to Baljeet. He told the teacher we were copying." The others nodded. Mohit felt strong, like the captain of a winning team.

Wednesday. Baljeet sat alone at lunch. Mohit watched his friend Aman look at Baljeet's lunch box, then at Mohit. Mohit felt a flicker of fear. What if Aman went to Baljeet's side? Then Mohit would be the one on his own. So he said loudly, "Anyone who sits with him is out too."

Friday. Aman sat with Baljeet anyway. Two more boys followed. Mohit stood with his tray and nobody beside him. For a moment, he knew exactly how Baljeet had felt all week.

qa.q: Why did Mohit say nobody should talk to Baljeet?
qa.a: He said Baljeet told the teacher they were copying.

qa.q: What was Mohit afraid of on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was afraid that if Aman went over to Baljeet, he himself would be the one left alone.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Mohit, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Standing alone with his tray showed him how Baljeet had felt; he could apologise to Baljeet and join Aman's table.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt choosing to sit with Baljeet?
qa.a: Aman was probably nervous about Mohit's threat but felt it was wrong to leave Baljeet alone, and Aman's choice gave others courage.

grounding: A boy organises a freeze-out of a classmate, feels powerful, and acts from fear of losing his own place, until he ends up alone.

passage: Rania, fifteen, noticed it in her school in Dubai before anyone else seemed to. Aiko, who had moved from Osaka in January, used to sit with a group from art class. Now she ate lunch on the bench by the car park, reading the same page of a book. When Rania checked the class group chat, she saw that a new chat for the art trip had been started, and Aiko wasn't in it. Rania didn't want to make a scene; that would only embarrass Aiko. So on Monday she took her sandwich to the car-park bench and sat at the other end. "Do you know how to shade glass? I'm useless." Aiko looked up. She did know. By Thursday, when Rania's teacher asked students to pick partners for the mural, Rania said, "Aiko and me," before anyone else chose.

qa.q: Where had Aiko started eating lunch?
qa.a: She ate lunch on the bench by the car park.

qa.q: Why did Rania decide not to make a scene?
qa.a: She thought a big fuss would only embarrass Aiko, so she chose a quiet way to include her.

qa.q: Which of Rania's small acts helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Aiko about shading glass gave her a real reason to talk, and choosing her for the mural included her without drawing attention.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel when Rania picks her for the mural?
qa.a: Aiko would likely feel relieved and wanted, after weeks of eating alone and being left out of the trip chat.

grounding: A teenager notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from a group chat, and includes her through small, quiet acts.

passage: At the chess academy's residential camp, meals were served in a long hall, and the regulars always took the same tables. Jatin, sixteen, noticed that Zainab, the new girl from Hyderabad, had eaten alone for four days, hunched over her pocket chess set. In the camp's group chat, everyone else was tagged in the evening blitz plans; she never was. Jatin didn't announce anything. At breakfast on Friday, he carried his plate to her table and asked, "Can you show me what you did in that endgame yesterday? I couldn't follow it." She could, and explained it with her fork and pepper shaker. That afternoon, when the coach asked students to pair up for analysis, Jatin said, "Zainab and I." Nobody seemed to notice anything unusual. By evening she had been added to the blitz chat.

qa.q: What was Zainab hunched over while eating alone?
qa.a: She was hunched over her pocket chess set.

qa.q: What does Jatin's quiet approach suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to include Zainab without drawing attention to her loneliness, which might have embarrassed her.

qa.q: Which small act worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking about her endgame and pairing with her for analysis gave Zainab a natural way to join in, which led to her being added to the chat.

qa.q: How might the other campers see Zainab after that day?
qa.a: They may start to see her as part of the group and a strong player, rather than the quiet girl eating alone.

grounding: A teenager notices a new camper eating alone and left out of chats, and includes her through small acts that break the cycle quietly.

passage: Avni, twenty, found out on a Sunday morning: her four closest college friends had gone to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park, and she hadn't been invited. The photos were everywhere. She sat on the edge of her bed and let herself cry. "This hurts," she wrote in her journal. "It doesn't mean I'm broken." That week she messaged Manoj from her NSS unit, who always saved her a seat at the tree-planting drives. "Chai after the drive on Saturday?" He replied with a thumbs-up. They talked for two hours about their villages and bad hostel food. She joined his Sunday reading group too. When one of the old group asked her for notes later, Avni thought about saying no, as they had to her. She sent them anyway.

qa.q: Where did Avni's friends go for the birthday dinner?
qa.a: They went to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when she found out, and how did she see herself?
qa.a: She was deeply hurt and cried, but told herself the hurt did not mean she was broken.

qa.q: What choice did Avni make when her old friend asked for notes, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She sent the notes anyway instead of excluding them back, which kept her from becoming like the people who hurt her.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Avni's message about chai?
qa.a: Manoj would likely be pleased to be asked, since he already saved her a seat, and glad to spend time with her.

grounding: A young woman excluded by her friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others, and chooses not to retaliate with exclusion.

passage:
"You've been staring at that phone for an hour, Vinita." Zeenat sat down on the other bed in their hostel room.
"They made a new group for the Goa trip. I'm not in it."
"The four from your class?"
"Yes." Vinita's voice cracked. "I thought we were close."
Zeenat put an arm round her.
"That really hurts."
"It does. And I keep thinking, what's wrong with me?"
"Nothing's wrong with you. Maybe something changed with them. That's not the same thing."
Vinita wiped her eyes. "My birthday's next week. I could just not invite them either."
"You could. Would it make you feel better?"
Vinita thought. "No. It would make me like them."
"Come to my theatre group rehearsal tomorrow. They're a mad bunch, you'll like them."
"Okay." Vinita put the phone face down. "And I'll invite who I want, not who I'm angry at."

qa.q: What trip was the new group made for?
qa.a: The new group was made for the Goa trip.

qa.q: What was Vinita worried about when she said 'what's wrong with me'?
qa.a: She was worried that being left out meant there was something wrong with her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's thinking?
qa.a: When Zeenat asked if not inviting them would help, Vinita realised it would only make her like them, and chose not to retaliate.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see Vinita's hurt?
qa.a: Zeenat takes it seriously, telling her it really hurts and nothing is wrong with her, and offers a new group to join.

grounding: A young woman excluded from a friend circle admits the hurt, refuses to blame herself or retaliate, and reaches out to new people.
